shortlist.premise: A clock preserving reference time can help locate a ship east or west by comparison with local solar time.
shortlist.stop: A clock answers a question we associate with a map.
shortlist.payoff: Understand why a time difference can represent longitude.
hooks: How can a clock tell a ship where it is?
Two places, two noons: the difference reveals east or west.
Before GPS, one crucial piece of navigation was keeping time.
shortlist.visual: Compare a ship's local noon with carried reference time, then reveal a rotating Earth relationship; an object-led historical scene or restrained explanatory map are possibilities.
shortlist.evidence: Royal Museums Greenwich supplies both the mechanism and Harrison history; later use instrument/trial records and an independently checked illustrative calculation.
shortlist.uncertainty: Solar time versus civil time, sign convention, practical observation and chronology need careful scoping; Harrison was not the only method.
shortlist.production: A clock and globe can become decorative unless the viewer sees the actual comparison; avoid an astronomy scale ladder or a dense navigation lesson.
shortlist.history: Touches Earth/physics and engineering, but replaces the old scale comparisons and traffic simulation with a historical problem and a time-to-position reframe.
shortlist.advance: Proposed first choice: immediate, resolvable contradiction, accessible museum path and a strong explanation; narrow to the principle, not the whole longitude contest.
shortlist.arc: Ship lacks an east–west reference → local noon differs from the carried reference clock → time difference becomes an angular position → keeping a clock reliable at sea mattered.
verify: Check local apparent/mean solar time distinction and a simple longitude example.
Check what the chosen historical timekeeper actually did; avoid exclusive-inventor or instant-adoption claims.
Separate illustrative navigation from measured trial evidence.

shortlist.premise: In an asymmetric-information model, buyers' uncertainty can make selling a good used car unattractive and degrade the market.
shortlist.stop: Bad products can push good ones away without physically outperforming them.
shortlist.payoff: Understand adverse selection as an information problem rather than a slogan about dishonesty.
hooks: Why can good used cars disappear from a market?
What happens when the seller knows something the buyer cannot see?
A low offer can remove the very cars buyers hoped to buy.
shortlist.visual: Reveal concealed good/bad qualities and a buyer's pooled offer, then show a good-quality seller leave; object-based dramatization or an original marketplace example, without advice.
shortlist.evidence: Akerlof's Nobel autobiographical explanation and Nobel lecture lead to the original 1970 paper; direct Nobel page opens returned 403, so feasibility is excerpt-level.
shortlist.uncertainty: The mechanism depends on assumptions about information, reservation values and offers; it is not a claim that all used-car markets collapse.
shortlist.production: A numerical demonstration can overload a phone or imply a universal outcome; the before/after mix must be internally consistent.
shortlist.history: Shares money with Billion Dollars and cars with Phantom Traffic, but neither cash scale nor traffic flow is the subject; hidden information drives the story.
shortlist.advance: Finalist for a useful mental model; source access and abstract explanation make it less immediately secure than longitude.
shortlist.arc: Seller knows quality → buyer discounts unknown quality → good seller declines → remaining mix worsens; finish on information changing what gets traded.
verify: Retrieve the original paper and distinguish theoretical example from empirical market outcomes.
Check a minimal example's prices, values and assumed buyer knowledge.
State that certification, warranties and other institutions can change the result without making recommendations.

shortlist.premise: Historical European women often used pockets tied around the waist under clothing, rather than only pockets sewn into garments.
shortlist.stop: A familiar clothing complaint opens into an unexpected physical object.
shortlist.payoff: See how detachable storage worked and why modern pocket history is more complicated than a single missing-feature story.
hooks: These pockets were separate from the dress.
Where did you keep your belongings before pockets were sewn into the garment?
The hidden bag underneath historical clothing.
shortlist.visual: Reveal a tie-on pocket through a clothing cutaway or original object reconstruction; show access through a slit and actual storage rather than a costume slideshow.
shortlist.evidence: V&A object-backed article plus its cited Burman/Fennetaux scholarship and collection records; images are copyrighted and not production-cleared.
shortlist.uncertainty: Dates, geography, class and access designs vary; surviving garments do not justify an all-women/all-history claim or a simple conspiracy about pocket removal.
shortlist.production: An original cutaway must accurately represent construction; museum image rights and costume detail could slow the most attractive reveal.
shortlist.history: No historical Magnivis video explains clothing or lived material culture; object-scale illustration serves use and social context instead of a size record.
shortlist.advance: Finalist with the freshest everyday-object surprise and likely discussion; payoff must explain function rather than merely reveal an old accessory.
shortlist.arc: Recognizable pocket question → detached object reveal → show tying, concealment and access → reframe pockets as portable possessions and independence within a specific historical setting.
verify: Check a specific dated object and documented wearing/access arrangement.
Scope period and European geography; avoid universal claims about women.
Separate documented contents/functions from historical interpretations of autonomy.
Establish an original or licensed visual path.

shortlist.premise: Conservation imaging helped identify a section of Magritte's missing The Enchanted Pose underneath another painting.
shortlist.stop: A supposedly lost artwork can be present inside an artwork already on display.
shortlist.payoff: Understand how physical clues and image matching turn conservation into a detective story.
hooks: The missing painting was hiding under another painting.
Why did conservators turn this X-ray sideways?
A clue at the canvas edge opened a second picture.
shortlist.visual: A layered canvas, edge clue and rotated imaging reveal; later use permission-cleared evidence or an explicitly labeled schematic rather than fabricated X-rays.
shortlist.evidence: MoMA conservators' firsthand 2013 account provides an unusually direct discovery path; current museum records are needed before extending the story to all pieces.
shortlist.uncertainty: The 2013 report found half, not the final state of the entire search; motives for repainting were speculative.
shortlist.production: Exact artwork and imaging rights could be decisive; schematic substitution may lose the emotional reveal. Nude figures also require proportionate presentation.
shortlist.history: A genuine art mystery with an evidence-led reveal, unlike every registered scale/mechanism video; do not imitate a frog thaw as a generic concealed-layer gimmick.
shortlist.advance: Finalist for the strongest detective reveal; held below longitude/pockets until present-state and rights feasibility are checked.
shortlist.arc: Lost picture → unexpected edge/UV clue → X-ray rotated and matched to a known reproduction → the object survived as a painted-over fragment.
verify: Check current status of all identified fragments; do not narrate a 2013 open question as today's mystery.
Separate observed matching from speculative motive.
Confirm reproduction/imaging rights and any ethical presentation decisions.
Keep dates and artworks distinct.

shortlist.premise: Donor–recipient pairs that cannot donate directly may be matched with other pairs through kidney exchange.
shortlist.stop: Two blocked acts of generosity can sometimes unlock each other.
shortlist.payoff: Understand a matching system in which finding compatible relationships matters more than setting prices.
hooks: You cannot donate to your loved one—but another pair may help.
Two impossible donations can sometimes become possible together.
A market designed without buying the organ.
shortlist.visual: Pair relationships and compatibility connections, with calm human-centered storytelling; original schematic and no surgery or emotive patient fabrication.
shortlist.evidence: Roth Nobel lecture and award speech are leads; later transplant program/clinical eligibility sources and legal scope needed. Speech opens failed.
shortlist.uncertainty: Real eligibility, compatibility, chains, timing and jurisdiction rules are more complex than blood-type arrows.
shortlist.production: A clean two-pair diagram could misrepresent certainty or medical eligibility; represent a hypothetical and avoid patient outcomes.
shortlist.history: Human Engineering covers structures, Wood Frog physiology; this is social/clinical coordination, with no biological-recovery spectacle.
shortlist.advance: Serious shortlist candidate but not final five: resonance is excellent; medical scope and institutional detail raise the burden for this cycle.
shortlist.arc: A blocked donor pair → another blocked pair → compatible crossing connections → matching enables exchange.
verify: Obtain program-authoritative explanation of compatibility and eligibility.
Determine jurisdiction and whether a simple cycle or chain is the intended example.
Avoid treatment advice, guarantees or invented patient stories.

shortlist.premise: Kwolek's decision to test an unusual cloudy polymer solution led toward the development of Kevlar.
shortlist.stop: A result that looked wrong became valuable when someone investigated it.
shortlist.payoff: See discovery as noticing and testing an anomaly, with a material mechanism beyond a motivational anecdote.
hooks: The solution looked wrong. She tested it anyway.
What did a cloudy liquid have to do with a strong fiber?
A material breakthrough began with an unexpected laboratory result.
shortlist.visual: Contrast expected versus observed liquid behavior and follow the tested solution into fibers; labeled reconstruction or object-focused material explanation, no violent test.
shortlist.evidence: Smithsonian Lemelson search excerpt and ACS biography offer converging institutional leads; later oral history, papers/patents and team-development chronology needed.
shortlist.uncertainty: No invented quotes or near-discard scene; polymer alignment and strength comparisons need specific experimental scope. ACS popular wording is not ballistic evidence.
shortlist.production: Liquid/fiber depiction must avoid suggesting the liquid itself has fiber strength or that one person instantly invented finished body armor.
shortlist.history: Distinct person-led invention story; shares materials/engineering with Human Engineering but focuses on an anomaly and decisions rather than structure dimensions.
shortlist.advance: Finalist for a concrete human story with explanatory depth; ranks behind longitude because a satisfying mechanism may need chemistry compression and stronger primary history.
shortlist.arc: Unexpected solution → deliberate test → unusually useful fiber → why noticing an anomaly changed the material's path, with team work acknowledged.
verify: Check chronology and attribution against primary history/patents/oral accounts.
Check solution behavior versus final fiber properties.
Avoid universal bulletproof, strength or steel-comparison claims.
License any archival objects/images; do not use the AI-enhanced ACS portrait as historical evidence.

shortlist.premise: In susceptible saturated sediment, earthquake shaking can build pore-water pressure and reduce strength.
shortlist.stop: The ground can lose support without the mineral grains melting.
shortlist.payoff: Understand a support mechanism and why soil conditions matter, rather than seeing a disaster clip.
hooks: The sand does not melt. So why can the ground behave like a liquid?
What happens between wet sand grains during shaking?
shortlist.visual: Cross-section of grains, water and load; a safely bounded conceptual demonstration is possible later, not disaster footage.
shortlist.evidence: USGS susceptibility explainer and New Madrid program mechanism; primary geotechnical work later for precise stress description.
shortlist.uncertainty: Not every wet soil liquefies; density, drainage, shaking and stress conditions matter.
shortlist.production: Grain animation could imply all ground turns to water; disaster spectacle would undermine explanation.
shortlist.history: Earth/nature adjacency to Ocean Depth, mechanism differs; risk of repeating Phantom Traffic's emergent-system diagram grammar unless story gives a reason.
shortlist.advance: Strong mechanism reserve within shortlist, outside final five because the chosen explanation resembles recent hidden-system work and needs careful portrayal.
shortlist.arc: Apparent solid support → shaking changes pressures → grain contact support weakens → explain susceptibility.
verify: Scope saturation/density conditions and effective-stress explanation.
Review illustrative representation of pore pressure.
Avoid geographic hazard predictions or emergency advice.

shortlist.premise: Silbo Gomero conveys a whistled form of Spanish, encoding speech rather than only attention signals.
shortlist.stop: A whistle can carry linguistic content rather than just a call.
shortlist.payoff: Understand how a different acoustic channel preserves enough language to communicate with context.
hooks: That whistle carries words.
How can you send a sentence across a valley without shouting?
shortlist.visual: A mountain communication context, a permission-cleared real speaker sample and a modest spoken/whistled comparison; no AI imitation masquerading as authentic speech.
shortlist.evidence: Max Planck Dutch-language explanation opened; UNESCO indexed heritage description is a lead, direct open gave a JavaScript/bot challenge.
shortlist.uncertainty: Phoneme counts/encoding explanations vary; translation and participant claims must be checked with specialist evidence.
shortlist.production: Authentic intelligible audio, translation and rights are central; invented whistles would defeat the premise.
shortlist.history: First language/heritage subject; sound-led rather than default narrator-and-diagram treatment, but execution remains undecided.
shortlist.advance: Excellent shortlist option; not final five due to audio authenticity/rights and specialist translation needs.
shortlist.arc: Hear a whistle → reveal linguistic content → show reduced acoustic encoding and context → appreciate a living communication tradition.
verify: Check an authentic translated example with a competent speaker.
Distinguish whistled Spanish from a separately invented language.
Check current practice and phonetic descriptions without repeating outdated universal superlatives.

shortlist.premise: Magnetic core memory stored bits in tiny rings threaded with wires, with much assembly performed by hand.
shortlist.stop: Something as abstract as computer memory once depended on microscopic manual threading.
shortlist.payoff: Understand a bit as a physical magnetic state and acknowledge skilled manufacturing labor.
hooks: Computer memory used to be threaded by hand.
Each of these tiny rings could hold a bit.
shortlist.visual: Macro object view to one ring's magnetic state and wire paths; original schematic or rights-cleared artifact imagery, not an instant code-to-cloth metaphor.
shortlist.evidence: Computer History Museum explains magnetic states, manufacture and competing inventor histories; artifact/patent documents later.
shortlist.uncertainty: Core RAM is distinct from core-rope read-only memory; do not merge assembly anecdotes, Apollo attribution or exclusive invention claims.
shortlist.production: True wiring/read-destructive behavior can overwhelm a short; fake wire geometry risks teaching the wrong mechanism.
shortlist.history: First computing manufacturing story; different from large structures but has a familiar small-to-large visual temptation that is optional.
shortlist.advance: Clear shortlist contender; outside finalists because the strongest opening is physical labor while the mechanism can add too much detail.
shortlist.arc: Hand-threaded object → single ring/bit → wires change and read state → connect abstract computing to physical work.
verify: Choose one real core RAM artifact and verify assembly practice.
Distinguish core rope and core RAM.
Scope invention attribution and any read/write explanation.

shortlist.premise: DART's asteroid collision provides a real example of deflection in which ejected material contributes to momentum transfer.
shortlist.stop: Material flying away can add to the push on what remains.
shortlist.payoff: Understand recoil and momentum transfer rather than merely hearing that NASA hit an asteroid.
hooks: The spacecraft was only part of the push.
Why can debris flying away move the asteroid more?
shortlist.visual: Impact and outgoing ejecta with separate motion arrows, plus a bounded before/after orbital comparison; original or licensed imagery, simulations labeled.
shortlist.evidence: NASA mission page and JPL March 2026 result provide discovery and timely context; later primary papers for momentum enhancement and system-orbit distinctions.
shortlist.uncertainty: Dimorphos' orbit around Didymos differs from the system's orbit around the Sun; enhancement is target-specific, not guaranteed planetary defense.
shortlist.production: A dramatic impact can imply explosion or saved Earth; orbital scale and before/after magnitudes are easy to exaggerate.
shortlist.history: Returns to space after Earth to Stars/Speed of Light but explains intervention/recoil rather than cosmic scale; domain repetition alone does not disqualify it.
shortlist.advance: Strong shortlist timely alternative; below final five because it risks news framing and requires multiple orbit/measurement distinctions.
shortlist.arc: Impact → ejecta carry momentum away → recoil contributes to asteroid motion → what a tested deflection establishes and what it does not.
verify: Retrieve relevant original experiment and 2026 analysis; separate measured outcomes and models.
Distinguish orbital period, heliocentric motion and momentum enhancement.
Confirm date/context at research time; no current-threat claim.
